title: Combining Conditions: AND, OR, NOT
learningObjectives: Explain how AND, OR and NOT combine or reverse Boolean results.
Evaluate compound conditions using truth tables.
Apply short-circuit evaluation to predict expression behaviour.
Build compound conditions for practical requirements.
Identify common mistakes involving precedence, parentheses and logic.

understand.concept: Logical operators combine or modify Boolean values. AND is true only when both operands are true; OR is true when at least one operand is true; NOT reverses a Boolean result. A compound condition can express several requirements in one decision.
understand.whyItMatters: Real rules often contain multiple requirements or alternatives. Combining conditions lets programs represent eligibility, validation, access rules, ranges and decision criteria without writing a separate decision for every possibility.
understand.analogy: Imagine entering a venue: you need a valid ticket AND an age requirement, while a different event might accept a student pass OR a staff pass. NOT can express that a restricted area is not open.
understand.analogyLimit: Real policies can have exceptions and precedence rules. A simple logical expression should not replace careful interpretation of the full policy.

explain.narrative: AND (&& in JavaScript) requires both operands to be true. OR (||) requires at least one true operand. NOT (!) reverses a Boolean value. Parentheses group conditions and make intended order clear. In JavaScript, && and || short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated only when needed to determine the result (AND stops when the left side is false; OR stops when the left side is true). Logical operators have precedence rules, but explicit parentheses improve readability. Avoid confusing AND with OR, negating the wrong group, or mixing conditions without grouping. Truth tables help test every Boolean combination. This lesson uses JavaScript syntax for examples, while the underlying ideas are common across programming languages.

examples.title: AND: both requirements
examples.code: const hasTicket = true; const ageAllowed = false; console.log(hasTicket && ageAllowed);
examples.explanation: AND returns true only when both values are true. The second requirement is false, so the combined result is false.

examples.title: OR: either option accepted
examples.code: const hasStudentId = false; const hasStaffId = true; console.log(hasStudentId || hasStaffId);
examples.explanation: OR is true when at least one operand is true, so the staff ID is sufficient in this example.

examples.title: NOT: reverse a condition
examples.explanation: NOT reverses false to true. The result expresses that the place is not closed.

examples.title: Grouped conditions
examples.code: const age = 20; const hasPermission = false; const allowed = (age >= 18 && hasPermission) || age >= 21; console.log(allowed);
examples.explanation: The first group is false because permission is missing; the age-only alternative is also false because age is below 21.

examples.title: Short-circuit prevents a second check
examples.code: const user = null; console.log(user && user.name); console.log(true || console.log('not evaluated'));
examples.explanation: The && expression stops at the falsy left value and returns it; the || expression stops at true. The second console.log is skipped. JavaScript logical operators return operand values, not always a Boolean.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Eligibility rule
guidedTask.instructions: A member can enter if they have a valid pass AND their account is active. Predict the result for all four combinations of these two Boolean values.
steps: Create test cases: true/true, true/false, false/true, false/false.
Predict the outcome of each case.
Compare your predictions with the truth table.
guidedTask.starterCode: const hasPass = true; const accountActive = true; const canEnter = hasPass && accountActive; console.log(canEnter);

independentTask.title: Independent: Multiple accepted paths
independentTask.instructions: Create a rule where a user can access a resource if they are an administrator OR have a valid membership AND their membership is active. Group the membership conditions with parentheses and test at least four combinations.
requirements: Use parentheses to show the intended grouping.
Test cases that exercise each path.

hints: AND requires every operand to be true.
OR needs at least one true operand.
Use a truth table to test combinations systematically.
Parentheses make grouped logic clear and prevent precedence mistakes.
Short-circuiting may skip evaluation of the right operand.

questions.prompt: When is an AND expression true?
options: Only when both operands are true
questions.answer: Only when both operands are true
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions to be true.

questions.prompt: What does OR require to return true?
questions.explanation: OR returns true when one or more operands are true.

questions.prompt: What does NOT do to a Boolean true value?
In JavaScript, when does a false left operand make && skip its right operand?
options: When the left operand is falsy
Only when both operands are strings
questions.answer: When the left operand is falsy
questions.explanation: AND short-circuits when its left operand is falsy because the final result is already determined.

questions.prompt: Why are parentheses useful in a compound condition?
options: They show intended grouping and improve clarity
They remove the need for Boolean values
They make every operator run in reverse
questions.answer: They show intended grouping and improve clarity
questions.explanation: Parentheses make the logic explicit and help avoid precedence errors.
